extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, judges, and advanced law students working on §101 issues
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of whether claimed inventions satisfy 35 U.S.C. § 101 (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and the related judicial exceptions (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas), with focus on transitory signals and information-based inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories under §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter is limited to inventions that fall within one of the four statutory categories: 'process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be directed to at least one of these categories; the scope of §101 is defined by these categories but analysis often focuses on the essential characteristics of the claimed subject matter rather than forcing it into a single pigeonhole. Citation: 35 U.S.C. § 101; State Street Bank v. Signature Financial Group discussed as focusing on essential characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'manufacture' (American Fruit / Chakrabarty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'manufacture' has been quoted as 'the production of articles for use from raw or prepared materials by giving to these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations' and alternatively as 'anything made for use from raw or prepared materials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedent has used these dictionary-based definitions to interpret 'manufacture.' The concurrence emphasizes these definitions are 'expansive' and should not be read to impose a tangibility or permanence requirement. Use these definitions to assess whether claimed matter is 'made by man' and has new form/quality/use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility/permanence is not a prerequisite (concurrence view)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention need not be non-transitory or permanently tangible to be a 'manufacture' or composition of matter; transitory, unstable, or non-isolatable intermediates have been held patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically exclude transitory phenomena (e.g., propagating signals) from §101 on the basis of fleeting existence alone. Precedents cited: In re Breslow (transitory chemical intermediates patentable), In re Hruby (pattern over time patentable). Evaluate whether the claimed subject has 'some physical carrier of information' or an overall pattern/form created by human ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 'new' requirement distinct from §102 novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'new' in §101 is not merely the novelty assessed under §102; §101 requires that the subject matter be a creation 'made by man' rather than a mere discovery of a pre-existing natural phenomenon or abstract truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim is novel under §102, it can fail §101 if it seeks to claim a natural phenomenon, law of nature, or abstract idea. Use Funk Bros., Benson, and Chakrabarty to distinguish discoveries (unpatentable) from man-made inventions (patentable).

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 'useful' requirement (specific/substantial utility and attenuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter must be 'useful'—utility must be specific and substantial and not too attenuated from what is actually claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed subject has practical specific benefits in its currently available form (Brenner; In re Fisher). The 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' language (Alappat/State Street) is an indicator but not dispositive. Consider whether the utility is merely an asserted end-use remote from the claimed abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas / mathematical algorithms exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas (including pure mathematical algorithms) are not patentable subject matter under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Gottschalk v. Benson and Parker v. Flook show that an algorithm or mathematical relationship, even if novel, can be unpatentable if the claim would effectively monopolize the abstract idea. Determine whether the claim attempts to patent the algorithm/principle itself or an application of it to a new and useful end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on essential characteristics rather than form of claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry should look to the essential character of the subject matter rather than merely which of the four categories a claim is drafted into.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a claim must be drafted to at least one statutory category, courts advise examining the invention's essential characteristics (State Street Bank). Avoid letting claim drafting form (e.g., drafting as a signal vs. a storage medium) determine patentability (Flook warning against 'draftman's art').

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter doctrine and functional relationship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Information or 'printed matter' on a substrate lacks patentable weight unless there is a new functional relationship between the printed matter (information) and the substrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only distinction from prior art is the information content without a new functional relationship to the medium, the information often lacks patentable weight (In re Gulack). The printed matter rejection is often treated under §103, but may be relevant to §101 'useful' analysis. Lowry is an example where data structures imparted a physical organization and tangible benefits, distinguishing them from mere printed matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between claims to information and to medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying inventive contribution should be analyzed consistently whether claimed as information/signal alone or encoded on/contained in a tangible medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not permit a claim to a storage medium containing information to be patentable while denying patentability to the same information when claimed as a signal simply because one is encoded on a tangible substrate. Evaluate the invention's substance: is the human ingenuity the same regardless of claimed form? (Concurrence argues this distinction is incoherent; PTO historically treated Beauregard-style claims as patentable.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Application-of-principle vs. monopolization of principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimant must show an application of a law of nature or abstract principle to a new and useful end rather than monopoly over the principle itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funk Bros., Benson, and Flook articulate that inventions applying natural laws or algorithms may be patentable when tied to a specific, useful application. Evaluate whether the claim would preempt all uses of the underlying principle or merely claim a particular application with tangible benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims involving mental processes/algorithms require machine tie or creation of composition/manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim that involves mental steps or algorithms may qualify as statutory subject matter if it is tied to a machine or creates/involves a composition of matter or manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'machine-or-transformation' style reasoning (cited via Comiskey and related authorities): if a claimed process is tied to a particular machine or effects a transformation or creation of a composition/manufacture, it is more likely to be within §101. This is relevant when evaluating claims that are primarily algorithmic or mental in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and purposive interpretive approach to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of 'manufacture' and related §101 terms should be sensitive to historical usage and the constitutional and statutory aim to promote the 'useful arts'—Congress intended wide scope for patent laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult contemporary and historical dictionary meanings and constitutional context (useful arts/technology) rather than relying solely on modern common-sense meaning. Chakrabarty counsels a broad reading ('anything under the sun made by man') subject to exceptions, so limit exclusions to the well-established judicial exceptions (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas).
